The Complete Guide to WebSocket Reconnection

By Alex Rivera · March 14, 2026 · 9 min read

WebSocket connections fail. They fail when laptops close their lids, when phones wander between cell towers, when corporate proxies decide that ninety seconds of idleness is suspicious, and when a load balancer quietly recycles the backend your socket happened to be pinned to. A connection that has been open for an hour is not evidence that it will be open one second from now. Any production system built on WebSockets therefore needs a reconnection strategy that is deliberate rather than accidental, and the difference between the two is the difference between a product that feels alive and one that silently goes stale while the user keeps typing into the void.

This guide walks through the full lifecycle of a robust reconnection layer: how to detect that a connection has actually died, how to schedule retries without stampeding your own servers, how to resynchronize state once you are back, and how to communicate all of this to the human staring at the screen. The advice here is battle-tested across browser extensions, mobile clients, and server-to-server meshes, and although the code samples use the browser WebSocket API, every pattern translates directly to ws libraries in Node, Python, or Go.

The first and most underrated problem is detection. TCP is designed to survive silence, which means a dead connection often looks identical to a quiet one. If the remote peer vanishes without sending a FIN — a yanked cable, a suspended laptop, a NAT table that expired — your socket object will happily report itself as open for minutes or, in pathological cases, forever. The close event you are waiting for may simply never arrive. The only reliable cure is an application-level heartbeat: the client sends a small ping frame on a fixed interval, the server echoes a pong, and the client treats a missing pong within a timeout window as a death sentence. Keep the interval generous enough not to burden mobile radios — fifteen to thirty seconds is typical — and keep the timeout at roughly twice the interval so a single delayed packet does not trigger a false positive.

Backoff, jitter, and the thundering herd

Once you know the connection is dead, the temptation is to reconnect immediately and retry in a tight loop until it works. This is how you turn a sixty-second server deploy into a self-inflicted denial-of-service attack. When a popular service drops ten thousand clients at once and all ten thousand retry on the same fixed schedule, the reconnection spikes arrive as synchronized waves that can keep a recovering backend pinned to the floor. The industry-standard answer is exponential backoff with jitter: each consecutive failure doubles the base delay, and a random factor spreads the actual retry instants across the window so the herd never stampedes in step.

A good implementation also distinguishes between failure modes. A socket that connected successfully and then dropped after ten minutes deserves a fast first retry — the network blip is probably already over. A socket that has failed its handshake five times in a row should be backing off toward a ceiling of thirty or sixty seconds. Resetting the backoff counter only after the connection has proven itself stable for some grace period, rather than immediately upon connecting, prevents a flapping link from oscillating between instant retries and long waits.

  • Start with a base delay of about one second and double it on every consecutive failure.
  • Cap the delay at a sane ceiling — thirty to sixty seconds for interactive apps.
  • Apply full jitter: pick a uniform random delay between zero and the current cap.
  • Reset the counter only after the new connection survives a grace period, not at the moment of connecting.
  • Stop retrying entirely on fatal errors such as authentication rejection, and surface those to the user instead.

Here is a compact reference implementation of the scheduling core. It is deliberately framework-free; the same twenty lines have shipped inside browser extensions and Electron apps alike:

class Reconnector {
  constructor(connect, { base = 1000, cap = 30000 } = {}) {
    this.connect = connect;
    this.base = base;
    this.cap = cap;
    this.attempt = 0;
  }
  schedule() {
    const exp = Math.min(this.cap, this.base * 2 ** this.attempt);
    const delay = Math.random() * exp; // full jitter
    this.attempt += 1;
    this.timer = setTimeout(() => this.connect(), delay);
  }
  markStable() {
    // call after the socket has been healthy for a grace period
    this.attempt = 0;
  }
  stop() { clearTimeout(this.timer); }
}

Notice what the class does not do: it never inspects the close code itself. Deciding whether a disconnect is retryable is policy, and policy belongs to the caller. Close code 1000 after an explicit logout should not trigger a retry; close code 1006 after a network change almost always should. Keeping the scheduler dumb and the policy explicit makes both halves trivially testable.

Resynchronizing state after reconnect

Reconnecting the transport is the easy half. The hard half is answering the question the application immediately asks: what did I miss? If the server pushes incremental updates — chat messages, presence changes, document operations — a client that was offline for forty seconds has a gap, and pretending otherwise leads to the most painful class of bugs: state that is silently, persistently wrong. The three workable strategies, in increasing order of sophistication, are full refetch, sequence-numbered replay, and server-side session resumption. Full refetch is crude but unbeatable for correctness: on every reconnect, throw the local cache away and ask for the world again. Sequence numbering tags every server push with a monotonically increasing id; the client sends the last id it saw during the handshake and the server replays the gap from a ring buffer. Session resumption moves the burden entirely server-side, keeping per-client cursors alive for a grace window so the reconnecting client appears, from the application's point of view, never to have left.

Whichever strategy you choose, queue outbound messages while disconnected and flush them after resync completes — not before, or your messages may reference state the server has since invalidated. Cap the queue and tell the user when it overflows. An honest "reconnecting, 3 messages pending" badge beats a silent buffer that discards work. The table below summarizes the trade-offs we have observed in production deployments of each approach.

StrategyServer costClient complexityGap correctnessBest for
Full refetchHigh per reconnectTrivialPerfectSmall state, rare drops
Sequence replayRing buffer memoryModeratePerfect within windowEvent streams, chat
Session resumptionPer-client cursorsLowPerfect within TTLCollaborative editing
Ignore the gapNoneNoneWrongPure ephemeral data only

One final piece deserves more attention than it gets: telling the user the truth. A connection indicator with three honest states — connected, reconnecting with a countdown, and gave-up-retry-manually — converts a frustrating mystery into a comprehensible situation, and gives the user an explicit lever to pull instead of a page reload of last resort. Pair the indicator with the browser's online and offline events to skip pointless retries while the machine knows it has no network at all, and you have covered the overwhelming majority of real-world disconnection scenarios with perhaps two hundred lines of deliberate code. The patterns are not glamorous, but they are the difference between software that degrades gracefully and software that quietly lies about being alive.
